morphology.summary: An organelle, not a cell: a double-membrane-bound structure of eukaryotic cells that is the cell's power plant. A smooth outer membrane encloses a narrow intermembrane space and a deeply folded inner membrane; the inner membrane's folds (cristae) multiply its surface area and carry the respiratory-chain complexes and ATP synthase that convert the energy of nutrients and oxygen into ATP. It carries its own small circular genome and its own bacterial-type ribosomes, a legacy of its origin as a free-living bacterium engulfed by an ancestral cell roughly 1.5-2 billion years ago (endosymbiotic theory / serial endosymbiosis theory).
morphology.kind: double-membrane-bound organelle of eukaryotic cells (absent from bacteria and archaea, which lack membrane-bound organelles altogether)
morphology.size: Roughly 0.5-1 um in diameter and 1-2 um (up to ~4 um) long in a typical section - about the size and shape of a single bacterium, which is exactly what it evolutionarily is. A single cell can hold hundreds to thousands of mitochondria; the poster figure uses 2 um as a representative length.
morphology.shape: Classically drawn as a bean/sausage/rod shape in a static TEM cross-section, but in living cells mitochondria are dynamic, often elongated, branching and constantly fusing and dividing (fission/fusion) into networks or long tubules rather than sitting as isolated ovals.
morphology.outer_membrane: A smooth, continuous, unfolded phospholipid bilayer forming the organelle's outer boundary. Studded with porin (VDAC) channels that make it freely permeable to ions and small molecules (<=5000 Da), so its chemical environment is similar to the cytosol. Smooth is the key visual point: it must read as a single unbroken line with NO folds, in contrast with the inner membrane.
morphology.intermembrane_space: The narrow gap between outer and inner membranes, continuous in composition with the cytosol via the porous outer membrane. This is where protons pumped by the respiratory chain accumulate, building the electrochemical gradient that drives ATP synthase. In a drawing it is a thin, even, unbroken channel running all the way around between the two membranes - it must stay continuous, not pinch shut or vanish in places.
morphology.inner_membrane: A separate, far less permeable phospholipid bilayer richly packed (>70% protein by mass) with respiratory-chain complexes I-IV and ATP synthase. Thrown into deep, finger-like or shelf-like infoldings called cristae that project into the matrix. The flatter part of the inner membrane running parallel to the outer membrane (not folded into a crista) is called the inner boundary membrane; cristae connect to it through narrow, tubular crista junctions. This inner membrane, cristae included, is ONE continuous, unbroken sheet - the cristae are folds OF it, not separate pieces.
morphology.cristae: The signature structure. Deep folds/invaginations of the inner membrane that project into the matrix and dramatically increase the membrane surface available for oxidative phosphorylation (up to ~3x the cell's total membrane area in a liver cell). Their shape ranges from flat lamellar shelves to tubular/finger-like folds depending on cell type; cristae number and density scale with a cell's energy demand (about 3x denser in a cardiac muscle cell than a liver cell). CRITICAL: cristae must (a) clearly originate from and stay physically CONTINUOUS with the inner membrane at a narrow crista junction, never appear as free-floating plates or shelves detached inside the matrix, and (b) project INTO an interior space (the matrix) that is fully enclosed by the outer membrane - never open to the outside of the organelle.
morphology.matrix: The dense, gel-like interior space enclosed by the inner membrane. Contains the enzymes of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle and fatty-acid oxidation, dissolved ions, and - notably for this poster - the mitochondrion's own genetic machinery: several copies of circular mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) organised into nucleoid clusters, and hundreds of mitochondrial ribosomes (mitoribosomes). The matrix must be drawn as a single, fully enclosed compartment (never open, never leaking, never breached by the outer membrane) with cristae visibly projecting into it from the surrounding inner membrane.
morphology.mitochondrial_dna: A small, circular (NOT linear) double-stranded DNA molecule, ~16.6 kb in humans, present in multiple copies (typically several to tens of copies) clustered into small nucleoid bodies within the matrix, usually attached to the inner membrane. Encodes only 37 genes (13 respiratory-chain proteins + rRNAs + tRNAs); the vast majority of mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported. Inherited maternally (through the egg cell's cytoplasm) in the overwhelming majority of cases. This circular loop is the single most important visual cue for the endosymbiotic-origin teaching point and must be drawn as a small tangled RING, never a straight line or an X-shaped chromosome.
morphology.mitoribosomes: Ribosomes of bacterial type (70S-like, distinct in size and composition from the 80S ribosomes of the surrounding eukaryotic cytosol) that sit free in the matrix, often near the inner membrane and near mtDNA nucleoids, translating the handful of proteins mtDNA encodes. Draw as small dark granules/dots scattered in the matrix, distinct from - and typically smaller/sparser than - the free ribosome dots one would draw in a cytosol scene.
morphology.atp_synthase: Mushroom/lollipop-shaped F1F0-ATP synthase particles studding the cristae membrane on its matrix-facing side (a small round F1 head-piece on a short stalk seated in the membrane), where the proton gradient drives ATP production. Classic EM negative-stain images show these as tiny knobs/particles lining the cristae surface. A handful of these small stalked knobs along the cristae membranes is a nice, scientifically accurate detail; they must sit ON the cristae membrane (matrix-facing side), never floating free in the matrix.
morphology.colour_note: A mitochondrion has no colour in life; TEM images are greyscale. All colour in a teaching illustration is a convention chosen to make compartments legible - not the organelle's real colour.

structures.note: Single smooth unfolded boundary bilayer with porin channels. Must read as ONE unbroken line, with no folds - the cristae belong to the inner membrane only.
The thin, continuous gap between outer and inner membranes, running unbroken all the way around; where the proton gradient for ATP synthase is built up.
A second, separate, protein-rich bilayer, thrown into deep folds (the cristae). One continuous sheet with the cristae - never a separate structure from them.

THE signature structure. Deep folds of the inner membrane projecting into the matrix, multiplying the surface for the respiratory chain. Must stay CONNECTED to the inner membrane at a narrow crista junction - never drawn as detached free-floating shelves/plates inside the matrix.
The narrow neck where a crista connects back to the inner boundary membrane. Optional but useful detail for making the 'cristae are folds, not separate pieces' point unmistakable.
The dense interior space fully enclosed by the inner membrane, filling around and between the cristae. Must be a single, closed compartment - never open to the outside, never breached.

structures.la: filamentum anulare acidi desoxyribonucleici mitochondrialis (nucleoides mitochondriales)
structures.en: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), a small circular loop
structures.de: Mitochondriale DNA (mtDNA), eine kleine ringförmige Schleife
structures.note: A small tangled RING sitting in the matrix, drawn clearly circular (never linear/X-shaped). The key visual proof of the organelle's bacterial ancestry - inherited only through the mother, via the egg cell.
Small dark granules scattered in the matrix near mtDNA and the inner membrane - bacterial-type (70S-like), distinct from the cell's own 80S cytosolic ribosomes.
Tiny mushroom/lollipop-shaped particles (round head on a short stalk) studding the cristae membrane on its matrix-facing side, where the proton gradient drives ATP production.
Optional fine detail: small channel proteins dotting the outer membrane, making it freely permeable to small molecules.

do_not_draw: Do NOT draw a single membrane. A mitochondrion is ALWAYS double-membraned: a smooth outer membrane plus a separately folded inner membrane, with a visible intermembrane space between them.

Do NOT draw the cristae as detached, free-floating shelves or separate plates loose inside the matrix. They must stay physically CONTINUOUS with the inner membrane - folds OF it, connected at a narrow crista junction, not islands.

Do NOT leave the matrix open or unenclosed. The cristae project INTO a matrix that is fully enclosed by the inner membrane; the interior must never appear breached, leaking, or open to the space outside the organelle.
Do NOT draw a nucleus inside it: no double envelope with nuclear pores, no nucleolus, no chromatin. The mitochondrion is not a miniature cell with its own nucleus.
Do NOT draw the mitochondrial DNA as a linear strand or an X-shaped chromosome. It is a small, closed, circular loop - draw it as a tangled ring, always circular.
Do NOT give it a bacterial cell wall, capsule, flagellum, pili or fimbriae. It descends from a bacterium but is now an organelle with only its two membranes - no bacterial surface appendages.

Do NOT draw stacked green thylakoid discs/grana. That is a chloroplast's internal membrane system (a different organelle, from a different endosymbiotic event) and a common confusion with cristae - cristae are infoldings of a single continuous inner membrane, not separate stacked discs.

Do NOT anthropomorphise it in the textbook/sem/3d/watercolor styles: no face, eyes or limbs there (a friendly face is fine ONLY in the separate coloring-book page). No text, letters, numbers, scale bars, arrows-with-labels or watermarks baked into any image.

Do NOT draw uniformly sparse or absent cristae - the folded inner membrane multiplying the surface area is the entire visual point of a mitochondrion; too few or too shallow folds reads as a generic blob, not a mitochondrion.

colour_legend.outer_membrane: #4A6FA5 (steady mid-blue), drawn as a single thin smooth line
colour_legend.intermembrane_space: #DCE6F2 (very pale blue), the narrow gap between outer and inner membrane
colour_legend.inner_membrane: #C0392B (warm brick red), same colour for the inner boundary membrane and every crista fold - visually ties them together as one continuous sheet
colour_legend.cristae: same #C0392B as inner_membrane (they are the same structure); crista lumen a slightly paler rose
colour_legend.matrix: #F3E3C3 (warm cream/tan), fills the enclosed interior around and between the cristae
colour_legend.mitochondrial_dna: #E8B93A (golden yellow), a small tangled ring, high-contrast against the cream matrix so it reads instantly
colour_legend.mitoribosome: #5C6B73 (slate teal-grey) small dots, distinct from the golden mtDNA ring and from the reddish cristae
colour_legend.atp_synthase: #7FB37F (soft green) tiny lollipop knobs dotting the cristae membrane on the matrix side
colour_legend.porins: #4A6FA5 slightly darker flecks on the outer membrane, same hue family as the membrane itself
colour_legend.note: The mitochondrion has no colour in life and TEM is greyscale; every colour here is teaching convention. The palette's job is to make the double-membrane / cristae-connected-to-inner-membrane / enclosed-matrix relationship legible at a glance, and to make the golden mtDNA ring pop as the endosymbiosis teaching hook.

sources.title: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell - 'The Mitochondrion' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK26894)
sources.note: Canonical account: double membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae that project into the matrix and greatly increase surface area (about a third of total cell membrane in a liver cell), cristae density scales with energy demand (3x denser in cardiac vs liver mitochondria).

sources.title: Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach - 'Mitochondria' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9896)
sources.note: Inner membrane is the principal ATP-generation site, >70% protein by mass, houses oxidative phosphorylation machinery and metabolite transporters; matrix holds ~67% of mitochondrial protein including the citric-acid-cycle enzymes, mtDNA and mitoribosomes.

sources.title: Nomina Histologica Veterinaria (Terminologia Histologica-aligned) mitochondrion hierarchy
sources.note: Official Latin terms used verbatim: Membrana mitochondrialis externa/interna, Spatium intermembranosum, Crista mitochondrialis, Junctio cristae, Matrix mitochondrialis, Filamentum anulare acidi desoxyribonuclearis mitochondrialis (mtDNA loop), Ribosoma mitochondriale, and the F1-particle Caput/Stipes/Basis (ATP synthase headpiece/stalk/basepiece).

sources.title: Wikipedia - Crista
sources.note: Cristae are folds of the inner membrane, separated from the inner boundary membrane by narrow crista junctions, studded on the matrix side with F1 ATP-synthase particles - basis for the crista_junction structure and the ATP-synthase-on-cristae detail.

sources.title: Wikipedia - Inner mitochondrial membrane
sources.note: Confirms the inner membrane is differentiated into the inner boundary membrane (parallel to the outer membrane) and the cristae, continuous with each other at crista junctions - the basis for 'cristae are folds OF the inner membrane, connected, not detached shelves'.

sources.title: PMC - 'Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiont hypothesis: 50 years later'
sources.note: History and evidence for the endosymbiotic/serial-endosymbiosis theory: mitochondria descend from an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont taken up by an ancestral host cell, retaining their own circular genome and bacterial-type ribosomes as direct evidence of that ancestry.

sources.title: PMC - 'Mitochondrial Evolution' review (bacterial ancestry of the mitochondrial genome)
sources.note: The mitochondrial genome is of unquestioned bacterial ancestry within the alpha-Proteobacteria, a highly reduced descendant of a much larger free-living bacterial genome - supports the 'bacterium taken up long ago' teaching line.

sources.title: Creative Biolabs / mitoribosome structural literature summary
sources.note: Mitoribosomes are assembled in the matrix, rRNA components mtDNA-encoded, structurally related to but distinct from bacterial ribosomes - basis for calling mitoribosomes 'bacterial-type' rather than identical to bacterial ribosomes.

sources.title: biancahoegel.de - Mitochondrium (German cell-biology reference)
sources.note: German terminology check: äußere/innere Membran, Intermembranraum, Cristae, Matrix, mitochondriale DNA (ringförmig, ca. 1% der zellulären Erbinformation), Mitoribosomen; used to confirm natural German phrasing for the descriptions.

sources.title: MDPI/PMC - 'Mitochondrial Cristae Morphology Reflecting Metabolism...' review
sources.note: Confirms cristae morphology varies (lamellar vs tubular) by cell type and metabolic state, and that ATP synthase dimers concentrate at the highly curved crista rims/ridges - basis for showing ATP synthase knobs along the cristae membrane.
